Simon set the recovered drive on the bedroom table and waited for Esther to ask why its seal was broken.

The red candle flickered on the other side of the room like an accusation he already knew.

"You opened it," she said without looking up from the documents scattered across her workspace.

"I needed to verify."

"That's my job."

He crossed the room and set his hands on her shoulders, careful with the water-damaged prosthetic. "Yes."

Esther raised one brow at him. "You've never taken a job from me."

"Never."

She let herself be pulled to her feet. "Then why?"

Simon caught the falling book before it hit the floor. The wet prosthesis clicked softly on release. Esther met his eyes, and he waited for her next word.

She took the book and held it just beyond his reach.

"I was certain you'd give it back," she said, watching his other hand open at its limit.

The prosthetic clicked again. She dropped the book on his palm. The second time, it took Simon two clicks to release the new object—an empty water bottle with salt traces inside. His fingers kept moving without his willing them. The water bottle rolled across the table and stopped against an old photo of the two of them.

Esther took his good hand and guided it to the table, keeping it between them. Her nails were too long. He couldn't feel the cuticles beneath them, but he knew the shape by touch alone. She always kept that single nail longer than the rest.

"Show me," she said.

His hands hesitated for only a second. She closed his fingers over the photo, then another object: the envelope half-torn where water had loosened the seal. The contents were wet enough to hold a crease that wouldn't belong to paper this old. He recognized the torn edge and her fingernail print. The new damage had been intentional.

"You already saw it," she said softly.

The prosthesis clicked again.

Esther held the envelope out, then took his good hand in both of hers.

"Look at me," she said. "We have to look at them now."

He did. He took the envelope and set it aside. The red candle caught on a new line written over the old one. She'd dated it by name and date in her signature flourish. Simon thought of how quickly it had come together, how quickly they'd learned to read each other's injuries.

Esther came close enough to kiss him. Her lips were salt water and coffee from where she'd been working. He touched the scar on her thigh and felt the bruise beneath his hand.

"The new one," she said softly, lifting her skirt.

Simon touched the dark bruise on her skin. He had done that. He traced it with his hand. Her breath caught in his throat, and he realized his other hand was touching her scar.

Esther pulled him to the bed and knelt on top of him. Her hands moved him into position without speaking. He could feel the heat of her body between their legs.

"Wait," he said, breathing hard.

She stopped moving. The room around them blurred into bright edges and dark water. Esther's eyes held his while she pulled her skirt higher and let her weight press between them.

Simon reached up and held her hips in place. He could see the water dripping from her hair and the salt on her lips. Every movement felt like a promise made in the dark and kept in the light.

"Now," he whispered.

She moved down, slow enough to feel him enter her with the same certainty she'd shown when she opened the envelope. He touched the bruise again, felt her breath hitch, and held her hips steady while she took him deeper.

"Show me the rest," she said.

Simon pushed himself up so she could see where his hand had left its mark. The evidence of it made her skin flush bright against the bruise. He saw her eyes shift focus before her next word came.

"You have to know where it hurts now."

Her hands moved to guide him. The prosthesis locked again, and he bit his tongue to keep from crying out.

Esther slowed down. "Tell me."

His words came in parts: "Not here—the hand—the release button—."

She stopped moving. "I'm going to show you."

Simon watched her take the prosthetic in both hands. The release button clicked twice, and something small and red fell into her palm. His body responded before he understood what she was doing with it.

Esther smiled and moved closer. The candle caught between them, and he knew then what she would say next. "This one's yours."

She let the wax drip between their bodies while he came hard enough to scream.

The room brightened around them when they stopped. Simon realized Esther was still holding his palm. Her skin was warm enough to melt a little wax left on his hand from where she had set the candle down. The stain stayed for a few seconds longer, then disappeared under his thumb.

He looked up and caught her eyes in his.

"You'll take tomorrow," he said softly.

Esther nodded and took the red candle in her other hand. She held it up to the window. Outside, the city lights were coming on one by one.

"Yes," she whispered. "Together."

She set the candle on the table, and they watched the wax drip down while the room filled with their breaths.

Simon set the recovered drive on the bedroom table and waited for Esther to ask why its seal was broken.

She did not look at him. "This was supposed to stay closed," she said quietly, her eyes on the window. A single branch moved in the windless air.

"I—"

"It's done," Esther said, her voice hardening. Her body followed suit. Muscles clenched along her jaw, throat, shoulders. "Don't apologize. You did what you thought was right."

Simon reached out, hesitated, then put a hand on her shoulder. The muscle was rigid under his palm. "I know you'd never forgive me if I left it shut," he said. "But you're right—it had to be done."

Esther shook her head. "Not right," she said. "It had to be done. The cost is different. And this doesn't change my mind about letting them in."

She paused, swallowing hard before continuing. "It was never a question of you not knowing. It was a question of not wanting to know." Her fingers drifted upward, touching the wet spot on her shirt collar where he had pressed it too hard. "I couldn't ask you to watch and then take it all on yourself. That wasn't fair. Not then, not now."

The branch outside tapped against the window. In the sudden darkness of a cloud passing overhead, Simon caught sight of his reflection—the shadow of his hand reaching for her neck, his open palm, his outline blurred by the movement of rain.

He lowered his hand. "What about you?" he asked. "Will you watch now, when I'm done?"

The question hung between them like the branch, bending but not breaking in the windless night. Esther looked at her reflection, then at him. "Yes," she said finally. "I will watch now. Because it matters that we see this together."

She turned away, moving toward the small workroom she'd set up when the team arrived. Simon followed her in silence, keeping a careful distance between them as she lit the lamp and began to unpack her tools. The hum of electricity filled the small space; the ticking clock in the hallway marked each passing second.

Simon reached out again, brushing his fingers against the curve of her shoulder as she leaned over the work surface. "I can help you," he said gently, "if you'd like."

Esther nodded, her eyes still focused on the half-completed diagram spread across the table. Together they opened the drive, moving carefully as the light flickered and dimmed in one room while staying bright in the other.

The workroom clock ticked behind them as they reassembled the device. When it was finally complete, Esther drew a deep breath and plugged it into the nearest socket. Simon felt a familiar weight settle onto his chest—the weight of all those names he'd tried to protect, the weight of keeping her secret, the weight of letting her bear it alone.

"There's one thing I never told you," Simon said softly as she turned back toward him. "About how this was always supposed to end."

Esther looked up from the device. Rain against the window blurred Simon's features; the dim light left his expression unreadable.

"What did you never tell me?" she asked quietly, her voice breaking on the last word.

Simon reached out and closed her fingers around the handle of the small knife she kept in her workroom pocket. "This was always meant to be a choice," he said. "Yours, at the end. Like we both agreed."

She felt his warmth through the fabric, his touch lighter than air yet heavy with meaning. The weight of the knife felt solid in her hand, as if it belonged there.

"Are you sure?" Esther whispered, her voice thick with emotion.

Simon nodded once, firm and resolute. "Positive," he said. His eyes held hers, steady and unwavering in their certainty. He knew her pain, he knew her strength, and he trusted her judgment more than anyone else's.

They stayed that way for a long moment—him looking into her eyes, her gaze fixed on his reflection in the rain-streaked window behind him. When Esther finally turned away, Simon could see the small smile tugging at one corner of her mouth.

"Okay," she said softly. "Let's do this together."

Simon watched as Esther carefully undressed, his gaze never leaving hers in the dim light. When she was ready, he knelt beside her on the bed and took the knife from her hand, setting it down within easy reach. His touch lingered on her skin as he helped arrange herself for comfort.

"You know I'm going to stay here," Esther said quietly, her fingers brushing the curve of his jaw. "Even after this."

Simon nodded, his own eyes misting over with unshed tears. "I know," he whispered, tracing patterns along her bare shoulder. "It's okay. You'll always be safe with me."

They remained motionless in their shared silence, Simon holding Esther close as the rain continued to fall outside. The faint rhythm of raindrops on glass punctuated their quiet intimacy until dawn broke through the clouds and cast its gentle light across the room.

The shadow of her knife traced a new path on his back as Simon left the room, moving carefully through the thin strip of light that marked the doorway. His hand touched Esther's bare shoulder briefly before he disappeared into darkness again. The clock in the hallway ticked steadily, counting out time until their next meeting.

Esther watched Simon step through the beam of light to enter another room. The dark wet spot on his shirt caught her eye, a reminder of that morning's intimacy and the choice they'd made together. She reached her hand towards him as he crossed the threshold—the gesture meant for more than just this moment, an invitation for their next decision.

Simon set the recovered drive on the bedroom table and waited for Esther to ask why its seal was broken.

She didn't.

The drive had lain hidden for two years. Its contents held the proof he hadn't been able to protect. If she saw that now, his careful distance would become one more lie.

He took a breath instead of offering explanations. His fingertips rested on the smooth plastic case with its thin line of dried glue. Esther was tracing the scars across her lower back in the mirror, shoulders tense but otherwise still.

She turned and caught him looking at her nakedness as if it weren't the first time. "There is a point to your staring, yes?"

"Two points," he said. "Which would you prefer to address?"

Esther tilted her head. "Let us examine the easier option: when did I last see you naked?"

"Your wedding day."

"My mistake was assuming any day might be as good."

Simon pressed his lips together. When she was being witty, he never knew whether to laugh or touch her. He chose a third option: "Come here."

The bed creaked under both of them when she sat beside him. Her hand went to his chest, the touch feather-light on old scars she still remembered. "That wound was healing," she said. "When did you stop giving me reports?"

He let her fingers trace the puckered flesh and offered no correction. The truth was in front of him anyway.

"When we agreed that marriage required something other than careful observation."

"You decided this after I was separated for two years?"

"We had different plans. I wanted you safe. You wanted to come back."

Esther's hand stopped moving. Simon held her wrist gently and pressed a kiss to her palm. He could feel the decision trembling in her: stay angry or touch him back. She chose the second.

The warmth of her mouth met his lips with a weight that kept her close. Simon tasted wine on her breath. It made him remember why he kept bottles in the bedroom instead of the cellar, and why he never asked about the paper hidden beneath them.

His hand found the bottle wrapped in cloth, the heavy glass still holding warmth from a recent opening. He moved it to his lap without taking his eyes from hers.

"This came with the drive," he said. "The envelope was sealed with the same wax."

Esther's smile was slow and cautious. She took the bottle and turned it over in her hands.

"Do you wish to examine my handwriting first, or shall we discover this together?"

Simon's hand went to the seam in the cloth wrapping. His other hand moved to cup her face. Her skin was smooth and cool where his fingertips touched.

"Let us assume you are capable of deception." He pressed his mouth to hers again. "But perhaps not of the kind that matters."

The wine bottle made a small sound as he uncorked it, the noise mixing with their breathing. He poured carefully, filling two glasses with a deep red liquid that smelled more of earth than fruit.

They drank in silence, each glass warming slightly in their hands. Simon watched the way light caught in the wine's surface, creating small explosions of color where their fingers met.

"Shall we," he murmured, tilting his head toward the unopened envelope, "discover what a hidden message might reveal?"

Esther's eyes narrowed slightly. Her smile had shifted from cautious to speculative. She nodded once, her breath warm against his cheek as they leaned toward each other, hands closing around their glasses.

"Tell me again," she said softly, her voice dropping an octave lower, "that I am not worth preserving."

"Darling, you are worth every effort." His hand went to her thigh, moving slowly up her inner leg, the touch measured and deliberate. "And then some."

"Prove it."

Esther stood abruptly and Simon followed with the wine glasses, his heart racing despite years of experience. She locked the handcuffs on their wrists, pressing close enough for her heat to press against him. He could feel her breathing quicken as they stepped together.

She turned back to him, her eyes smoldering. "I want to hear you say it."

His hand found her bare hip, circling it gently with a weight that held rather than demanded. The cuffs jangled faintly against each other.

"I have always," he said, his voice rough from years of trying not to show feeling, "wanted you safe."

"More than anyone else?"

He pressed a kiss to the corner of her mouth, tasting wine there. "The only one."

Esther's lips curved into a smile that made Simon's pulse quicken despite everything. He could feel his cock hardening under his clothes as she stepped closer.

"You have not shown yourself capable of discretion," she whispered against his ear, her breath warm and sweet with wine. "Perhaps I should discover whether the contents warrant immediate destruction."

Her hand moved down, her fingers tracing his thigh as they circled the cloth that concealed the drive.

Simon's other hand went to hers, the cuffs connecting them. He tightened his grip slightly, holding her fingers still.

"I do not think," he murmured, his voice thick with the knowledge of what she was choosing not to ask, "that you will find anything there I have not already shown you."

She met his gaze steadily. Her hand moved again, the fingertips pressing against the rough surface of the hidden paper.

"Perhaps we should examine this matter together."

His breath caught as he watched her hesitation transform into a deliberate choice. His hand tightened on her waist, pulling her close enough for their bodies to brush. The wine glasses clinked slightly against each other as they pressed forward.

He reached carefully with his free hand, fingers wrapping around the edge of the cloth. Their breaths mixed in the warm space between them.

Simon pulled back the covering and found the paper unchanged under the wax seal. His heart picked up speed watching Esther's eyes take in what he had written. He could feel the moment she decided whether to remain his wife or become someone else entirely.

Her hand went to his cheek, her thumb tracing the scar that marked years of decisions made at other people's direction. The wax seal broke with a small, final sound as she moved it aside.

"This," she said softly, reading the paper he had written in precise, measured strokes, "was not your fault."

He closed his eyes and let himself feel what he hadn't allowed: the years of watching her, the silent planning that kept them together while everything else fell apart.

Simon opened his eyes to find hers filled with a new understanding. The paper slipped from her fingers and he caught it before it could touch the ground.

"I never wanted," he said quietly, his voice rough from the weight of all those words he hadn't spoken, "to make you choose between us."

The paper lay open between them, ink still visible where it had soaked through the page. He watched her read carefully, each word carrying more than what was written.

Esther's hand closed on his forearm. Her fingers pressed against his skin with a firmness that held meaning beyond words.

"I have," she whispered, her breath warm against his collar, "been choosing you all along."

Simon's hands found her hips without thinking. His thumb traced the scars that marked years of fighting for them both. The cuffs clinked faintly as they moved together.

They lay back on the bed in careful coordination, their movements measured against the paper still pressed between their arms. Simon could feel her breathing deepen as he watched her study their joined wrists, her fingers lingering over the scars where they touched.

She looked up at him with eyes that held everything they had never spoken about: "Your report was complete."

The paper crinkled slightly as he shifted to reach for the envelope. His hand moved over it gently, pressing the seal back in place before setting it aside.

"I wanted," he said quietly, his breath catching as they pressed closer together, "you to choose this with me."

She closed her eyes briefly, then opened them again with a smile that made him remember how they had met: "Consider it done."

The bed creaked faintly as he moved to kiss her neck, their bodies aligning with a precision that came from years of watching each other fight. His tongue found the pulse point there and tasted salt along with wine.

Esther's breathing changed as his hand moved beneath her shirt. She pressed closer, their hands still connected by the cuffs that kept them apart only in one way.

Simon set the recovered drive on the bedroom table and waited for Esther to ask why its seal was broken.

The salt had dried between his fingers into white dust.
Esther came to him at the door, her eyes tracking up his wet body until they stopped. Her hand raised as if to touch his chest but hesitated halfway.
“You went in,” she said.
“Yes.”
“And left the breach open.”
“Yes.”
Silence held them where the current had washed them.
Esther closed her eyes and pressed a palm against his wet chest. His pulse marked her skin.
“I thought you’d failed,” he said.
She let out a breath he hadn’t realized she was holding. “I did.”
“That’s why you never told me how close you were.”
“Yes.”
“And that’s why I didn’t fight to go in myself.”
“I don’t know. Why didn’t you, Simon?”
He turned away. The drive waited under the lamp like an accusation.
Esther followed him with one slow step. She held his gaze a breath longer before dropping her hand, leaving the weight of a question she wouldn’t press.
“That’s what I wanted to know,” he said quietly.
She looked down at her own hands for so long he thought she might not answer. Then, very deliberately, she touched him. Not at his chest but along the line of the scar where his skin had knit back together, closing a wound deeper than skin alone.
Her touch brought back the taste of blood and salt in his mouth, the red blur that had become their life. Her fingers traced the length of it, a pale scar against dark skin under lamplight, and when she reached its end, she kissed his neck without ceremony or hesitation.
The contact was brief but absolute, and when it broke, it left a shape behind it that couldn’t be hidden.
“How is it?” he asked.
“Healed,” she said, her voice low. “But not forgotten.”
“Nor this,” he said, turning his back to show the bruises his ribs still bore from the final engagement.
She traced those marks with equal care, naming them one by one as if committing them to memory.
“This is from the blast,” she said against his skin where the rib protruded slightly more than flesh alone should manage.
He made a sound in his throat. “I’ve been better.”
“We’ve been better,” she corrected. “But we’re still whole, Simon.” Her voice had lost its edge.
Her hand moved across his chest to where the prosthetic met flesh, and this time he didn’t pull away. He’d shown her worse scars than these, though none that held such weight between them as the knowledge that either could have failed alone and neither wanted to bear that burden again.
“This is yours now too,” he said softly, turning his head to catch her eye as she met flesh with metal where no skin remained. “All of it.”
“Yes.” Her voice was barely more than breath against his ear. “That’s why we’re here now.”
Her hands moved down his body without hesitation. The scar was no boundary but a threshold he’d chosen to cross when he chose her again.
They stood in that quiet room while the water from the dive dried slowly on his skin. She touched him exactly where she’d said she would and nowhere else. Her palm found its way beneath his shirt until their bodies pressed together more firmly than words could manage.
“You know I’d have come with you,” he said against the curve of her shoulder as her fingers explored the length of his scar. “I wouldn’t have left you alone.”
“I know,” she whispered, her breath warm against his neck. “But you didn’t know then. Neither did I. That’s why we keep doing this—because it matters that we’re still here together.”
Her hands moved lower along his torso until they found the weight of his prosthetic again. Her touch was matter-of-fact yet reverent; there was no shame in what remained nor glory either—just fact held between them like an answer given without question.
When she looked up at him again through wet hair and salt-dried skin, there was nothing uncertain in her eyes. Her hands moved deliberately but gently across his ribs where bruises still marked his skin. Her touch traced each line with equal care whether scar tissue or fresh injury.
“I’m not afraid of these,” she said quietly, pressing a palm to the tender spot where one rib protruded slightly beyond flesh alone should manage, “because they’ll heal and you’ll still be here.”
“And I won’t be afraid of yours because we’ll have new ones together tomorrow,” he answered, catching her wrist before she could pull away again.
Her smile held more weight than words could bear alone. The room remained dim except where lamplight fell on his chest and her hands as if marking territory claimed without resistance or question.
“You don’t need my permission for this,” he said softly against her shoulder when she drew back from tracing another line with her palm, “but I want you to have it anyway.”
Her fingers hesitated then traced the scar more firmly than before—the knowledge that his skin had knit itself back together beneath her touch visible in the way her hand trembled slightly as if bearing both proof and promise at once.
“Then let me do this,” she said quietly enough for only his ear to catch but clearly enough for neither doubt nor hesitation to follow in her voice or touch as she moved lower on his body where metal met flesh again with less caution than before as if claiming territory already yielded without question or regret.
Her hands found their way beneath his shirt once more until fabric no longer separated skin from metal—the boundary crossed deliberately without shame or glory but simply fact held between them like an anchor dropped in deep water where currents couldn’t shift it anymore.
“You still have questions,” he said, catching her wrist when she moved toward the scar tissue on his thigh with equal deliberate care, “but I don’t want you asking them while we’re apart anymore.”
“And I don’t want to answer them while I’m looking away from you either,” she said softly enough for only his ear to catch beneath salt-dried hair clinging stubbornly to skin still wet from seawater clinging stubbornly against light falling steadily across room dimming slowly toward darkness waiting outside windows thick with silence held between them until neither moved again.
“Then let’s finish this together,” he said quietly enough for only her ear to catch before moving both bodies forward into contact deeper than touch alone could manage until no boundary remained except choice freely given without question or hesitation holding fast against tides threatening still to separate what had been joined deliberately by choice freely made without fear or regret weighing heavy upon them both until neither moved again except together in motion deliberately chosen without question or hesitation following through until neither moved again.
Their hands found each other where no words could follow—metal met flesh where flesh met skin met metal where scar tissue knit back together beneath touch holding fast against tides threatening still but failing now utterly because neither would yield ground already gained deliberately by choice freely made without hesitation or question holding firm until neither moved again.
